title: Optimization Methods: GD, Newton, Momentum, RMSProp and Adam
description: From plain gradient steps to adaptive moments: what GD, Newton's method, Momentum, RMSProp and Adam each add to parameter updates.
content:
**Optimization** algorithms update a model's parameters step by step to minimize the loss function. The optimizers below form an evolutionary line: each one fixes a weakness of the previous one by adding new information or statistics to the update step.

The five methods compared:
• Gradient Descent (GD)
• Newton's method
• Momentum
• RMSProp
• Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)

**Gradient Descent (GD)** is a first-order optimization algorithm. It minimizes the loss function by iteratively adjusting the model parameters in the direction of the steepest descent of the loss gradient. The process repeats until the algorithm converges to a minimum of the loss function - a sign that the parameters are optimal.
• Uses only first-order information: the gradient.
• Cheap per step, but sensitive to the learning rate and prone to oscillating in steep valleys.

**Newton's method** introduces a second-order twist. It calculates the **Hessian** - the matrix of second derivatives - and multiplies the gradient by the inverse Hessian, adapting the update step to the curvature of the loss surface.
• Curvature-aware steps: bigger where the surface is flat, smaller where it is steep.
• In practice this approach is computationally ineffective and requires a lot of resources, since computing and inverting the Hessian is expensive for models with many parameters.

**Momentum** builds on GD by accumulating a moving average of past gradients - like a velocity that smooths the updates over time.
• Dampens oscillations, especially when the loss landscape has steep curvatures in some directions.
• Accelerates movement in directions where the gradient consistently points the same way.

**RMSProp** tackles the challenge of learning rate adjustment. It maintains an exponential moving average of the squared gradients for each parameter.
• Assigns a different learning rate to each parameter based on the historical magnitude of its gradients.
• Parameters that usually receive large gradients take smaller steps; parameters with small gradients take larger steps.

**Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam)** marries the ideas behind Momentum and RMSProp. It calculates an exponential moving average of both the gradients (the **first moment**) and the squared gradients (the **second moment**).
• First moment - direction with memory, as in Momentum.
• Second moment - per-parameter step scaling, as in RMSProp.

Summary:
• GD - steps against the plain gradient (first-order only).
• Newton - gradient scaled by the inverse Hessian (second-order, expensive).
• Momentum - adds velocity from past gradients.
• RMSProp - per-parameter learning rates from squared gradients.
• Adam - combines the first and second moments of both worlds.
